clue.text: East Anglian town, one mile by rail roughly-unlike this

parts.note: Diss is a small market town in Norfolk, in East Anglia
one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: roughly says the word rail is treated roughly, its letters jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: Directions to a small Norfolk town a mile down the railway line, contrasted with somewhere else.
explanation.walkthrough: DISS is a Norfolk town, not something British solvers abroad will know. 'roughly' turns RAIL into ILAR; 'this' at the end just points back to the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Two things that differ in kind are said to be unlike each other, a plain synonym.

clue.text: The fool who takes it

parts.note: a word for an idiot that also names a drug, and the drug is what the idiot takes

explanation.surface: Describing someone foolish enough to accept something.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word means an idiot and a narcotic, so the fool and the 'it' he takes share a name.
explanation.definitionFit: Dope is slang both for a stupid person and for drugs.

clue.text: Ducks in a way being somewhat smutty

definitions.note: the clue gives an adjective phrase for a noun, the black grime smut itself

indicators.note: in places the two zero shapes within the abbreviation for a road

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, shaped like O, so ducks are OO

explanation.surface: Waterfowl on a road, with a hint of something dirty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ducks' looks like birds, but in cricket a duck is a score of zero, written as the letter O; 'in' sets the pair inside the street abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Soot is the black powder from fires, and smut is the old word for such a sooty mark.

clue.text: Crop a chicken ruined, which ruined Ralph the Rover

indicators.note: ruined says the letters of the first phrase are wrecked and remade in another order

explanation.surface: A ruined bird crop and a pirate brought to grief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' scrambles CROP A CHICKEN. In Southey's ballad Ralph the Rover cut the warning bell from this reef off Scotland and later wrecked his own ship on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Southey's poem tells how the rover removed the reef's bell and was then drowned on that same reef.

clue.text: So esoteric, a barrister ?

definitions.meaning: known only to an ... circle, private
barristers belong to an Inn of Court such as the ... Temple, so a member is jokily one of its members

explanation.surface: Asking whether a lawyer is as obscure as his jargon.
explanation.definitionFit: Esoteric knowledge is private, for insiders, and a barrister belongs to an Inn of Court such as the Inner Temple.

clue.text: Meant perhaps to embrace Zeus's daughter for fun

indicators.note: to embrace puts the goddess inside the jumbled letters
perhaps indicates meant is only one possible ordering of its letters

parts.note: the nine Muses were daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne

explanation.surface: Intending to hug a Greek goddess for the fun of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges the given word to AMENT, and 'to embrace' wraps that round the goddess, just after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Amusement is enjoyment or entertainment, a synonym for fun.

clue.text: This ruler returned the ancient mariner's work

indicators.note: returned means the work's title is sent back the way it came, read from right to left

parts.note: Coleridge's poem is The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, so his work is a rime

explanation.surface: A monarch giving back a copy of Coleridge's famous sea poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns RIME, the archaic spelling of rhyme in Coleridge's title, into the ruler.
explanation.definitionFit: An emir is a Muslim prince or commander, a ruler in Arab lands.

clue.text: Folly being this kind of blunder ?

definitions.text: Folly being this kind of blunder ?

parts.words: Folly being this kind of blunder ?
parts.note: a folly is an ornamental tower or ruin, a kind of memorial building, and an enormous mistake is described by the related adjective

explanation.surface: Wondering just how big a foolish mistake can be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Folly' reads as foolishness, but here it is a showy ornamental building, a sort of monument; a huge blunder is called monumental.
explanation.definitionFit: Monumental describes a structure built as a memorial and, figuratively, any huge error.

clue.text: Born anew in a green tree, maybe

indicators.note: maybe says these letters might be arranged otherwise, so they are reordered

explanation.surface: New life springing up in a green tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' rearranges the letters of A GREEN TREE; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Regenerate as an adjective means spiritually reborn, as in a regenerate soul.

clue.text: Where curtain speeches are made, giving us nice change in a concert

indicators.note: in places the shuffled letters within the word for a concert

parts.note: a prom is a promenade concert, as at the BBC Proms

indicators.note: change asks for the letters of us and nice to be altered into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: An actor's farewell speech at a concert, with a fresh line about us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' turns US NICE into SCENIU, which goes 'in' PROM.
explanation.definitionFit: The proscenium is the stage front before the curtain, where an actor steps out to speak at the end.

clue.text: Athenian joiner's arms are reversed

definitions.note: Snug is the joiner among the workmen in A Midsummer Night's Dream, set near Athens; the 's stands for is

indicators.note: are reversed tells us the weapons word is written from its last letter back to its first

parts.note: arms are weapons, guns

explanation.surface: A carpenter in ancient Athens finds his coat of arms turned upside down.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's in 'joiner's' reads as 'is', so the joiner is GUNS turned around by 'are reversed'. 'arms' looks heraldic but means weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare names his Athenian joiner Snug, the craftsman who plays the Lion in the mechanicals' play.

clue.text: Underground dwelling for a gnome ?

definitions.meaning: a station on the London Underground, in north-west London
Swiss bankers are called the gnomes of Zurich, so one would live in an Alpine chalet-style house

explanation.surface: A gnome living in a hole below ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Swiss Cottage is a London Underground station; Swiss financiers are nicknamed the gnomes of Zurich.
explanation.definitionFit: The station is named after an Alpine-style cottage pub, and a Swiss gnome would live in a chalet.

clue.text: Rome in Gone With The Wind, say ?

definitions.text: Rome in Gone With The Wind, say ?

parts.words: Rome in Gone With The Wind, say ?
parts.note: Protestant polemic called the Church of Rome the Whore of Babylon, a woman in red; the heroine of the Margaret Mitchell novel is also a woman with that colour as her name

explanation.surface: A question about how the Eternal City figures in a famous Civil War novel and film.
explanation.walkthrough: Two readings: an old Protestant insult for the Roman church (from the woman in Revelation), and Scarlett O'Hara, the female lead of Gone With the Wind.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a biblical term for a loose woman, applied in polemic to the papacy, and literally fits the novel's heroine.

clue.text: According to us a conservative description of the charge

parts.note: acc. is the abbreviation for according
taken as written
a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A party member's view of the charges against them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link. The definition describes the charge as an adjective would: an accusatory charge.
explanation.definitionFit: An accusing tone is what you would call a charge or allegation, so the adjective describes it.

clue.text: How a blushing unseen flower dispenses its sweetness

definitions.text: How a blushing unseen flower dispenses its sweetness

parts.words: How a blushing unseen flower dispenses its sweetness
parts.note: Gray's Elegy says many a flower is born to blush unseen and squander its sweetness on the desert air

explanation.surface: A poetic question about how a hidden bloom spends its scent.
explanation.walkthrough: Gray's Elegy: 'Full many a flower is born to blush unseen, / And waste its sweetness on the desert air.'
explanation.definitionFit: To waste sweetness is to give it out pointlessly, with no one to enjoy it.

clue.text: Yet this wine gives real pleasure

definitions.text: Yet this wine gives real pleasure

parts.words: Yet this wine gives real pleasure
parts.note: the wine's name, said aloud, sounds like fake suffering, and the clue contrasts that with the true pleasure it gives

explanation.surface: Praise for a sparkling wine that genuinely delights.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, the wine's name is 'sham pain', false pain; 'Yet' sets that against the real pleasure.
explanation.definitionFit: Champagne is the sparkling French wine drunk at celebrations.

clue.text: Expressed by Francisco for relief at Elsinore

definitions.text: Expressed by Francisco for relief at Elsinore

parts.words: Expressed by Francisco for relief at Elsinore
parts.note: in the opening scene of Hamlet the sentry Francisco says For this relief much thanks

explanation.surface: A guard's words when his shift ends at the Danish castle.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet opens on the battlements of Elsinore; when Bernardo relieves him, Francisco says 'For this relief much thanks'.
explanation.definitionFit: Thanks expressed for being relieved of duty are a show of thankfulness.

clue.text: A piece of Japan, or an address in Spain

parts.note: a sen was a small Japanese coin, a hundredth of a yen, so a coin or piece of Japan
taken as written

explanation.surface: Picking between a fragment of Japan and a Spanish street address.
explanation.walkthrough: 'piece' means a coin, not a fragment, and 'address' means a form of address, a title, not a postal address.
explanation.definitionFit: Señor is the Spanish title for a man, the equivalent of Mr or sir.

clue.text: Give vent to one kind of rubbish

definitions.meaning: to voice or let out a sound or remark
in the phrase complete rubbish, a total kind of nonsense, the adjective means absolute

explanation.surface: Releasing pent-up feelings about a particular sort of garbage.
explanation.definitionFit: To give vent to is to say aloud, and total nonsense is called utter rubbish.

clue.text: Refined wit of an old sailor of Piraeus

definitions.text: of an old sailor of Piraeus
definitions.meaning: Piraeus is the port of Athens in Attica, and salt is slang for a sailor, so an Athenian seaman

explanation.surface: Praise for the elegant humour of a veteran seaman from the Athenian port.
explanation.definitionFit: Attic salt is a classical term for graceful Athenian humour, and literally an old sailor from Attica.

clue.text: Loving a face ?. Often it makes trouble

indicators.note: makes trouble tells us the preceding letters are stirred up and thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Musing on whether a pretty face invites trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes trouble' rearranges all the letters of A FACE OFTEN IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone affectionate shows fondness and warmth, which is to be loving.

clue.text: Bathing belle upset Scots lad with publicity

indicators.note: upset in a down clue turns the name over, so it is read from bottom to top

parts.note: Ian is the Scottish form of John, a typical Scottish boy's name
an ad is an advertisement, publicity

explanation.surface: A beauty in a swimsuit annoys a Scottish boy by courting the press.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' reverses IAN to NAI.
explanation.definitionFit: A naiad is a water nymph of Greek myth, a beauty who lives in streams, a playful bathing belle.

clue.text: Many in the ring seen on the floor

definitions.note: a description of a floor covering, standing in for the noun

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, many
a ring is shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A crowd at a boxing match visible on the canvas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Many' is a conventional hint for a Roman numeral, here L for fifty.
explanation.definitionFit: Linoleum is a floor covering, so it is what you see underfoot.

clue.text: It is I" the pirate is heard to say

indicators.note: is heard to say means the words are pronounced and we write what we hear

parts.note: the correct It is I is in everyday speech it's me, which ends in the sound 's me'

explanation.surface: A buccaneer announcing himself correctly.
explanation.walkthrough: Smee is Captain Hook's bosun in Peter Pan. Said casually, 'It is I' becomes 'it's me', and its last part sounds like his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Smee is the pirate boatswain on Captain Hook's ship in J M Barrie's play.

clue.text: Artistic section of Stock Exchange quotations?

definitions.text: Artistic section of Stock Exchange quotations?

parts.words: Artistic section of Stock Exchange quotations?
parts.note: the painter's medium shares its name with the market's petroleum shares listing

explanation.surface: Wondering which part of the share price list deals in the arts.
explanation.walkthrough: Painters work in oil paint, and on the Stock Exchange the shares of petroleum companies are listed together under the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: Oil paints are an artist's medium, and oil company shares form their own sector of market prices.

clue.text: Faith of a potential saint in a Jewish feast

indicators.note: in places the jumbled letters within the name of the feast

parts.note: Purim is the Jewish festival celebrating Esther's deliverance of the Jews

indicators.note: potential says saint is not yet in its final form, so its letters can be remade

explanation.surface: Someone who might become a saint attending a Jewish festival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'potential' turns SAINT into TANIS, placed 'in' PURIM.
explanation.definitionFit: Puritanism was the strict Protestant creed of the Puritans, a religious faith.

clue.text: Repeat — you have no end of fun with it

indicators.note: Repeat says the shortened word is said twice over
have no end says the final letter of you is removed

explanation.surface: An instruction to do something again, promising you endless fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'have no end' cuts YOU to YO, and 'Repeat' doubles it; 'fun with it' describes the toy.
explanation.definitionFit: The spinning toy on a string goes down and up for amusement, so it is something to play with.

clue.text: Interfering old law-maker, seldom troubled internally

indicators.note: internally puts the jumbled letters inside the word for the ancient lawmaker

parts.note: the laws of the Medes and Persians were proverbially unalterable, so a Mede is an ancient lawgiver

indicators.note: troubled signals the letters of seldom are disturbed into a new order

explanation.surface: A busybody veteran legislator who is only rarely bothered inside.
explanation.walkthrough: The Medes' laws could not be altered, hence 'old law-maker'. 'troubled' scrambles the word for rarely, which sits 'internally' just after the lawmaker's D.
explanation.definitionFit: A meddlesome person pokes into others' affairs, which is what interfering means.
